Window Restrictor Policy

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the window restrictor standard at every Alderbridge site. It applies to every
resident-accessible window above ground floor level.

Policy statement

A window restrictor is fitted to every resident-accessible window above ground floor level, limiting how far it
can open, protecting a resident from a fall risk while still allowing ventilation.

Definitions

**Window restrictor** a device limiting how far a window can open. **Resident-accessible window** a
window a resident could reach and open unsupervised.

1. Fit a window restrictor to every resident-accessible window above ground floor, limiting opening to
100mm.

2. Check restrictor function as part of the routine facilities inspection.

3. Report a damaged or missing restrictor to facilities immediately for urgent repair.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy works alongside the Health and Safety Policy and the Falls Prevention Policy.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the standard. A resident's first-floor room window is fitted with a restrictor
limiting opening to 100mm, allowing fresh air in while preventing the window from opening wide enough for
a fall risk.

Frequently asked questions

**Can a restrictor be removed for a window cleaning visit?** Yes, temporarily, by facilities, and refitted
immediately afterward. **Does a ground floor window need a restrictor?** Not under this policy, though a
specific resident's individual risk assessment may still recommend one.

Training and competency

Facilities staff are shown how to check and refit a restrictor correctly during induction.

Local and regional variations

A site with a particularly old window frame, such as an original sash window at Riverside House, may need
a bespoke restrictor fitting rather than a standard off-the-shelf model, arranged by facilities with a specialist
installer familiar with that window type.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the window restrictor standard at every Alderbridge site. It applies to every
resident-accessible window above ground floor level.

Policy statement

A window restrictor is fitted to every resident-accessible window above ground floor level, now limiting
opening to 65mm, tightened from the previous 100mm, following updated sector safety guidance.

Definitions

**Window restrictor** a device limiting how far a window can open, now to a maximum of 65mm.
**Resident-accessible window** a window a resident could reach and open unsupervised. **Quarterly
function check** the new mandatory check introduced in this version, confirming every restrictor still
functions correctly.

1. Fit a window restrictor to every resident-accessible window above ground floor, limiting opening to
65mm, tightened from the previous 100mm.

2. Complete a quarterly function check of every restrictor, a new mandatory requirement replacing the
previous informal check during routine inspection.

3. Report a damaged or missing restrictor to facilities immediately for urgent repair.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy works alongside the Health and Safety Policy and the Falls Prevention Policy.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the tightened limit. A resident's first-floor room window restrictor, previously
limiting opening to 100mm, is adjusted to the new 65mm maximum during the next quarterly check, and
the check itself is logged for the first time under the new mandatory schedule.

Window Restrictor Policy

Supersedes the version effective 1 June 2025. Adds a controlled emergency override key, held only by
senior staff, following a fire safety cross-check finding a restrictor could otherwise impede emergency
egress.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out the window restrictor standard at every Alderbridge site. It applies to every
resident-accessible window above ground floor level.

Policy statement

A window restrictor limiting opening to 65mm is fitted to every resident-accessible window above ground
floor level, now paired with a controlled emergency override key held only by senior staff, following a fire
safety cross-check finding a restrictor could otherwise impede emergency egress in a genuine emergency.

Definitions

**Window restrictor** a device limiting window opening to 65mm. **Emergency override key** the new
controlled key, introduced in this version, allowing a restrictor to be released quickly in a genuine
emergency. **Senior staff** the registered manager, deputy, or shift lead, the only roles holding an
override key.

1. Fit a window restrictor to every resident-accessible window above ground floor, limiting opening to
65mm.

2. Complete a quarterly function check of every restrictor.

3. Issue an emergency override key to senior staff only; this is a new control introduced in this version,
following the fire safety cross-check finding.

4. Use the override key only in a genuine emergency requiring rapid window access, such as a fire, never
for routine ventilation or cleaning.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This policy works alongside the Health and Safety Policy, the Falls Prevention Policy, and every
site-specific Fire Evacuation Procedure, which the override key now supports directly.

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the new override key. A fire safety cross-check identifies that a restricted
window could not be used as a secondary emergency exit route quickly enough in its current form.
Following this version, the shift lead's override key allows the restrictor to be released in seconds if
genuinely needed, addressing the finding without removing the restrictor's everyday fall-prevention benefit.

Frequently asked questions

**Why was the override key introduced?** A fire safety cross-check found the restrictor, while excellent for
fall prevention, could delay emergency egress through a window in a genuine emergency; the override key
resolves this without compromising everyday safety. **Can any staff member use the override key?** No,
only senior staff hold one, reflecting both the key's emergency-only purpose and the need to prevent
routine misuse.

Laundry Management Procedure

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how a resident's clothing and site linen is laundered at Alderbridge Care Group. It
applies to every site's laundry operation.

Policy statement

A resident's own clothing is laundered separately from site linen, clearly labelled, and washed at a
temperature appropriate to the fabric, while soiled linen follows a specific infection-control hot-wash
standard.

Definitions

**Resident's own clothing** clothing belonging to and worn by an individual resident, laundered separately
and returned to them. **Site linen** bedding, towels and similar items not tied to a specific resident.
**Soiled linen** linen contaminated with a bodily fluid, requiring the infection-control hot-wash standard.

Roles and responsibilities

**Laundry staff** launder a resident's clothing separately, labelled, and follow the correct wash
temperature for the item type. **Care staff** identify and bag soiled linen correctly for separate handling.
**The registered manager** ensures the laundry operation meets this procedure's standard.

1. Label every resident's clothing clearly on admission, and again promptly if a label is lost or becomes
illegible.

2. Launder a resident's own clothing separately from another resident's items and from site linen, at a
temperature appropriate to the fabric.

3. Wash soiled linen at 60 degrees Celsius, following the infection-control hot-wash standard, handled
separately from the point of collection.

4. Return laundered clothing to the correct resident promptly, checking labelling at the point of return.

5. Report a persistent labelling or mix-up issue to the registered manager for investigation.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a specific fabric or garment cannot tolerate the standard wash temperature (for example, a delicate
item), laundry staff use the manufacturer's care label instructions instead, recording the exception so it is
not treated as an error at the next audit.

A worked example illustrates separate handling. A resident's soiled bedsheet is bagged separately at the

fabric-appropriate temperature.

Frequently asked questions

**Can a family bring in their own detergent for a resident's clothing?** Generally no, since the site's own

used; a specific allergy concern is discussed individually with the registered manager. **What happens if
an item is genuinely damaged during laundering?** This is reported to the family honestly, and
Alderbridge's own policy on replacing a damaged item is applied.

Laundry staff complete training on separate handling, wash temperatures and the infection-control

The registered manager reviews laundry practice periodically as part of the wider infection control audit.

Managing a high laundry volume day

Following a resident group activity or an event involving several soiled items at once, laundry staff prioritise

happens to mention it again.

Laundry Management Procedure

Supersedes the version effective 1 May 2024. Introduces a barrier laundry system (one-way dirty-to-clean
flow) following an infection control audit finding, and tightens the soiled linen hot-wash temperature from
60 to 65 degrees Celsius.

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how a resident's clothing and site linen is laundered at Alderbridge Care Group. It
applies to every site's laundry operation.

Policy statement

A resident's own clothing is laundered separately from site linen, and the laundry room now follows a
barrier system with a strict one-way dirty-to-clean flow, with soiled linen washed at a tightened 65-degree
hot-wash standard.

Definitions

**Barrier laundry system** the new one-way flow, introduced in this version, physically separating a dirty
(soiled, incoming) zone from a clean (laundered, outgoing) zone within the laundry room. **Soiled linen**
linen contaminated with a bodily fluid, now washed at 65 degrees Celsius, tightened from the previous 60.
**Cross-contamination** the risk this version's barrier system is specifically designed to prevent.

Roles and responsibilities

**Laundry staff** follow the new barrier system, never carrying an item from the clean zone back into the
dirty zone or vice versa. **Care staff** identify and bag soiled linen correctly for separate handling into the
dirty zone. **The registered manager** ensures the laundry room's physical layout supports the barrier
system.

1. Follow the barrier system's one-way flow: an item enters the dirty zone, is washed, and exits only
through the clean zone, never returning to the dirty side; this is a new physical control introduced in this
version.

2. Label every resident's clothing clearly on admission.

3. Launder a resident's own clothing separately from another resident's items and from site linen.

4. Wash soiled linen at 65 degrees Celsius, tightened from the previous 60-degree standard, within the

5. Return laundered clothing to the correct resident promptly, checking labelling at the point of return.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a site's physical laundry room layout cannot fully separate a dirty and clean zone (for example, a
very small utility room), facilities arranges a strict time-based separation instead, cleaning and disinfecting
the space between a dirty-zone and clean-zone use, achieving the same cross-contamination prevention
principle through a different practical means.

Local and regional variations

A larger site with a purpose-designed laundry room, such as Harbour View, implements the barrier system
as two physically separate rooms, while a smaller site implements it as a single room with a clearly
marked, enforced one-way route.

either direction.

**Why was the barrier system introduced?** An infection control audit found the previous single-flow layout
created a theoretical cross-contamination risk between soiled and clean items; the one-way barrier system
removes that risk structurally rather than relying solely on staff practice. **Why was the hot-wash
temperature increased to 65 degrees?** Updated infection control guidance found 65 degrees provides a
more reliable margin against a resistant organism.

Laundry Management Procedure

Supersedes the version effective 1 May 2025. Adds a lost-item tracking log following recurring family

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how a resident's clothing and site linen, and reusable PPE, is laundered at
Alderbridge Care Group. It applies to every site's laundry operation.

Policy statement

A resident's own clothing is laundered separately within the barrier system, with a new lost-item tracking
log addressing recurring family concern about missing clothing, and reusable PPE now follows its own
dedicated laundering protocol distinct from resident clothing and general linen.

Definitions

**Barrier laundry system** the one-way dirty-to-clean flow protecting against cross-contamination.
**Lost-item tracking log** the new log, introduced in this version, recording every reported missing clothing
item and its resolution. **Reusable PPE** a washable apron or similar item, now laundered under its own
dedicated protocol rather than alongside general site linen.

Roles and responsibilities

**Laundry staff** follow the barrier system, complete the new lost-item tracking log entry for a reported
missing item, and follow the new dedicated reusable PPE protocol. **Care staff** identify and bag soiled
linen and reusable PPE separately for correct handling. **The registered manager** reviews the lost-item
tracking log monthly for a recurring pattern.

1. Follow the barrier system's one-way dirty-to-clean flow.

2. Label every resident's clothing clearly on admission.

3. Launder a resident's own clothing separately from another resident's items and from site linen.

4. Wash soiled linen at 65 degrees Celsius within the barrier system.

5. Log a reported missing clothing item in the new lost-item tracking log the same day it is reported,
including a description and last known laundry batch; this is a new requirement introduced in this version.

6. Launder reusable PPE using the new dedicated protocol, washed separately at a temperature and cycle

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a missing item cannot be located despite a full tracking log investigation, the registered manager

Local and regional variations

A site using a larger volume of reusable PPE, given a higher proportion of residents requiring more
frequent personal care tasks, dedicates a specific washing machine solely to the new PPE protocol rather
than sharing capacity with the general linen cycle.

Pest Control Procedure

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages pest control at every site. It applies to every site's kitchen, storage and resident areas.

Policy statement

Every site holds a contract with an approved pest control contractor providing a monthly inspection, with a clear reporting route for any staff member noticing a sign of pest activity between scheduled visits.

Definitions

**Approved pest control contractor** the vetted, contracted provider delivering scheduled inspection and treatment. **Sign of pest activity** any indication such as droppings, gnaw marks, or a sighting itself, reported regardless of how minor it appears.

Roles and responsibilities

**Facilities** manages the pest control contract and schedules the monthly inspection. **Any staff member** reports a sign of pest activity to facilities immediately on noticing it. **The pest control contractor** conducts the inspection and any necessary treatment, reporting findings to facilities.

1. Hold a current contract with an approved pest control contractor, providing at least a monthly site inspection.
2. Report any sign of pest activity to facilities immediately, regardless of how minor it appears.
3. Arrange an additional contractor visit promptly where a genuine concern is reported between scheduled inspections.
4. Keep food storage areas covered and clean as routine practice, reducing the conditions that attract pest activity in the first place.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where a confirmed pest sighting occurs in a food preparation area specifically, facilities treats this with particular urgency given the food safety implication, arranging same-day contractor attendance rather than waiting for the next routine visit.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This procedure works alongside the Catering and Menu Policy (governing food storage and preparation area standards) and the Waste Management Policy (governing waste storage, a common pest attractant if managed poorly).

Worked example
<<CHUNK>>

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This procedure works alongside the Catering and Menu Policy (governing food storage and preparation area standards) and the Waste Management Policy (governing waste storage, a common pest attractant if managed poorly).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates prompt reporting. A member of kitchen staff notices droppings in a storage cupboard between scheduled inspections. They report this to facilities immediately rather than waiting for the next monthly visit, and facilities arranges an additional contractor visit the same week to investigate and treat the area.

Frequently asked questions

**Does a single insect sighting need to be reported?** Yes, any sign is reported regardless of scale, since a single sighting can be an early indicator of a larger issue worth investigating. **Who decides whether a treatment is needed following an inspection?** The pest control contractor, based on their professional assessment of the inspection findings.

Training and competency

Kitchen and housekeeping staff are shown what to look for and how to report a sign of pest activity during induction.

Monitoring and compliance

Facilities reviews contractor inspection reports monthly, tracking any recurring finding at a specific site.

Record keeping and retention

Contractor inspection reports and any treatment record are retained per the Records Retention Schedule.

Seasonal awareness

Certain pests become more active during a specific season, such as a rodent seeking shelter as the weather turns colder; facilities and the contractor discuss a seasonal risk ahead of time so a site is not caught by a predictable, recurring pattern each year without having anticipated it.

Communicating with residents about a pest concern

Where a pest concern arises in a resident-facing area, staff communicate honestly and reassuringly with any resident who raises a question about it, explaining what is being done, since a vague or dismissive response can cause more anxiety than a clear, honest one.

Contractor access and site security

The pest control contractor is escorted or has agreed independent access arrangements consistent with the Contractor Management Policy, and facilities confirms their identity and booking before granting access to any resident area, since a pest control visit still requires the same access control discipline as any other contractor visit.

Pest Control Procedure

*Supersedes the version effective 1 June 2025. Adds a proactive prevention checklist covering bin storage and food waste as a distinct new requirement; adds an annual contractor performance review.*

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how Alderbridge Care Group manages pest control at every site. It applies to every site's kitchen, storage and resident areas.

Policy statement

Every site holds a contract with an approved pest control contractor, inspected fortnightly in the kitchen area, now supplemented by a proactive prevention checklist covering bin storage and food waste, with the contractor's own performance reviewed annually for the first time.

Definitions

**Approved pest control contractor** the vetted, contracted provider, now subject to an annual performance review. **Prevention checklist** the new proactive checklist, introduced in this version, covering bin storage, food waste handling and other conditions that attract pest activity, completed regularly rather than only reacting to a sign already found. **Annual contractor performance review** the new review, introduced in this version, assessing the contractor's own reliability and effectiveness.

Roles and responsibilities

**Facilities** manages the pest control contract, completes the new annual contractor performance review, and coordinates the new prevention checklist across relevant areas. **Any staff member** reports a sign of pest activity immediately and, where relevant to their role, completes the new prevention checklist for their area. **The pest control contractor** conducts inspection and treatment, now also subject to the annual performance review.

1. Hold a current contract with an approved pest control contractor, providing fortnightly kitchen area inspection and monthly inspection elsewhere.
2. Report any sign of pest activity to facilities immediately.
3. Log a confirmed rodent sighting the same day in the food safety log.
4. Complete the new prevention checklist for bin storage and food waste areas on a regular schedule, addressing a condition that could attract pest activity before it becomes an actual sighting; this proactive step is new in this version.
5. Complete an annual review of the pest control contractor's own performance, considering inspection reliability, treatment effectiveness and responsiveness to an additional-visit request; this is a new requirement introduced in this version.

Exceptions and professional judgement

Where the annual contractor performance review identifies a genuine, significant shortfall, facilities considers retendering the contract rather than continuing with an underperforming provider simply because switching contractors involves some administrative effort.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This procedure works alongside the Catering and Menu Policy and the Waste Management Policy, which the new prevention checklist now cross-references directly for bin storage standards.

A worked example illustrates the new prevention checklist. A member of housekeeping staff completes the bin storage prevention checklist weekly, confirming bins are properly closed and the storage area is clean, catching a slightly damaged bin lid before it becomes an attractant, addressing a condition proactively rather than waiting for an actual pest sign to prompt action.

**Why was a prevention checklist added when reporting and inspection already existed?** A review found most pest issues traced back to a preventable condition, such as poor bin storage, that existed for some time before an actual sign was noticed; the checklist catches the condition itself rather than only its eventual consequence. **What happens if the annual contractor review finds a problem?** Facilities addresses it directly with the contractor and, if unresolved, considers retendering the contract.

forward-looking development; the new name better reflects both halves of its purpose, and the process
itself has not changed. **What happens if a staff member disagrees with their review outcome?** They can
raise this through the normal grievance route if informal discussion with their line manager does not
resolve it.

Training and competency

Line managers complete supervision and review skills training, refreshed every two years, covering how to
give constructive feedback, updated to reflect the renamed Annual Performance and Development
Review.

Monitoring and compliance

HR tracks supervision and Annual Performance and Development Review completion rates monthly
across all sites, escalating a persistent gap to the relevant regional manager.

Record keeping and retention

Supervision notes and Annual Performance and Development Review records are retained in the staff
member's personnel file per the Records Retention Schedule.

Approval and review history

This policy was originally approved by the Chief Executive on 1 January 2025 and this version took effect
1 January 2026, superseding the earlier version's terminology.

Preparing for supervision as a staff member

Staff are encouraged to come to supervision with their own topics ready, whether a practical question, a
wellbeing concern, or an idea for improving practice, since supervision works best as a genuine two-way
conversation rather than a one-directional check from the manager alone.

Linking the review to career progression

Where a staff member expresses interest in progressing to a more senior role, this is discussed as part of
the Annual Performance and Development Review and reflected in the personal development plan,
identifying the specific training or experience that would support that progression rather than leaving the
ambition undiscussed until a vacancy happens to arise.

New manager induction into supervision practice

A newly promoted line manager receives additional coaching on conducting supervision well before taking
on this responsibility for the first time, since giving good supervision is itself a skill that benefits from
support rather than being assumed to come automatically with a management title.

Supervision for an agency or bank worker

A regular agency or bank worker who covers shifts consistently at a site is also offered a lighter-touch
supervision conversation periodically with the shift lead, distinct from the more formal Alderbridge
employment relationship they have with their own agency, since a worker who is a familiar, regular
presence still benefits from the same kind of reflective conversation as a permanent colleague.

Group supervision alongside one-to-one sessions

Some sites also hold an occasional group supervision session covering a shared practice theme relevant
to the whole team, such as a recent change in a care approach, which complements but never replaces
the individual one-to-one supervision each staff member is separately entitled to.

Confidentiality of supervision content

What is discussed in supervision is treated as confidential between the staff member and their line
manager, save where it raises a safeguarding, conduct or safety concern that must be escalated under the
relevant separate policy, and staff are told clearly at the outset where that boundary sits so they can speak
openly within it.

Supervision during a period of change

During a period of organisational change, such as a new care approach being introduced or a change in
site leadership, supervision frequency may be increased temporarily beyond the standard monthly
minimum, since staff typically need more, not less, individual support to adjust well during precisely this
kind of period, and a line manager is expected to recognise this need proactively rather than waiting to be
asked.

Closing note

Regular, genuinely useful supervision and an Annual Performance and Development Review benefit staff
and residents alike, and this policy exists to make sure both actually happen consistently rather than being
treated as a formality to complete.
